::: {.callout-note}
## In Layman's Terms

When you hit a golf ball in front of a launch monitor, the screen fills with numbers in a second: ball speed, launch angle, spin, club path, smash factor, and carry distance. All of those numbers look equally solid on the screen. They are not.

A launch monitor is either a fast camera sitting beside the ball, a radar unit sitting behind you, or a mix of both. A camera takes rapid pictures of the ball and club through a small window at impact. A radar bounces radio waves off the moving club and ball, the same way a police speed gun checks a car. Neither machine has a "smash factor sensor" or a "carry sensor." Each machine measures a few basic things and uses math models to work out the rest.

Smash factor divides ball speed by club speed. That cancels out most of what makes golfers different from each other: fast swingers and slower swingers end up with nearly the same smash factor. So in a group of good players, small shot-to-shot differences in strike, plus some measurement error, are enough to reshuffle who ranks highest from one week to the next. (For a quick guide on what to trust in practice, jump to @sec-practical-checklist.)
:::

::: {.callout-important}

## Observed Signals Versus Inferred State {#sec-observed-vs-inferred}

A launch monitor never sees a ready-made number called *club path* or *carry*. It records pictures or radio echoes and uses a mathematical recipe to turn them into numbers. Some recipes are straightforward geometry—like measuring your height with a tape measure. Others lean on physical assumptions—like working out your height from the length of your shadow and the time of day, where any error in your model of the sun ends up in your height.

In everyday golf conversation, launch monitors are split into a binary: "cameras measure at impact; radar tracks the flight." In control theory and **metrology** (the science of measurement), every instrument converts raw sensor signals into reported display numbers through a calibration and measurement model ([Launch Monitor Vendor Reference](../launch-monitor-vendor-reference.html)). In symbols, if $\mathbf{x}$ is the true physical motion of the club and ball, $\mathbf{z}$ is the raw signal recorded by the sensor, and $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is the list of numbers shown on the screen:

$$
\mathbf{z} = h(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{c}) + \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{y}} = g(\mathbf{z}, \hat{\mathbf{c}}, \mathcal{M}).
$$ {#eq-measurement-chain}

Here $h$ describes how the hardware senses the shot (using setup and calibration settings $\mathbf{c}$, such as camera lens geometry or radar tilt and target-line alignment, plus random sensor noise $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}$), and $g$ is the software recipe that turns the recorded signal $\mathbf{z}$ and estimated calibration $\hat{\mathbf{c}}$ into the displayed numbers $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ under a chosen physical model $\mathcal{M}$. Rather than asking whether a monitor "calculates" a number—every digital instrument calculates—an engineer asks three questions:

1. **What does the sensor actually see ($\mathbf{z}$)?** Is the box recording two-dimensional image pixels over microsecond flash exposures, or radio-frequency wave shifts over milliseconds?
2. **Is the recipe ($g$) direct geometry, or does it lean on a physical model ($\mathcal{M}$)?** Working out 3D ball speed from two calibrated camera views is direct geometry. Working out where the clubface pointed from where the ball started—without seeing the face—requires running an impact model backward. Predicting, for example, 270 yards of carry from a few feet of indoor ball flight requires running an aerodynamic flight simulator under assumed wind and air density.
3. **How sensitive is the recipe to small input errors?** When a displayed number $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is built by dividing two noisy numbers or running a model backward, its local sensitivity (the **Jacobian** $\partial g / \partial \mathbf{z}$, which tells how much the output moves per unit of input error) governs whether small errors cancel out or pile up.

This distinction between **observed outputs** and **inferred state** runs throughout AffineDrift's research programme, from [Launch Monitor Technology](../technology-launch-monitors.html) and [The Reference-Point Problem](../reference-point-problem.html) to [Interpretation of Inverse Dynamics](../inverse-dynamics.html).

## How the Two Architectures Sense the Shot {#sec-architectures}

### Stereoscopic Camera Monitors (For Example, Foresight GC2 and HMT) {#sec-camera-architecture}

A **photometric** (camera-based) launch monitor sits beside the ball, looking across the target line at a small impact window. Just as two human eyes judge depth because each eye sees the ball from a slightly different angle, a **stereoscopic** monitor uses two (or more) cameras spaced apart to triangulate the ball in three dimensions.

- **Hardware and raw signals:** According to Foresight Sports' product documentation (**manufacturer claim**; [What We Measure](https://www.foresightsports.com/pages/what-we-measure); [2023 Ball & Club Data Guide](https://support.foresightsports.com/sites/default/files/downloads/2023/2023%20Ball%20%26%20Club%20Data%20Doc.pdf)), the **Foresight GC2** uses two high-speed stereoscopic cameras ("Smart Camera System") to photograph the golf ball immediately after **separation** (the instant the ball leaves the clubface). A base GC2 observes only the ball. The optional **HMT** (Head Measurement Technology) add-on uses high-speed cameras aimed at the impact zone to track reflective markers stuck to the clubface (**manufacturer claim**).
- **Reconstructing ball speed, launch, and spin:** From two or more stereoscopic exposures separated by a known clock interval $\Delta t$, the software finds the 3D ball-center displacement $\Delta \mathbf{p}$ and divides by $\Delta t$ to obtain ball speed, vertical launch angle, and horizontal start direction (azimuth). To measure spin, the cameras photograph the ball's dimple or logo pattern across successive flashes to see how far the ball rotated and around which tilted axle (**spin axis**—the imaginary skewer the ball spins around, which tilts aerodynamic lift left or right to curve the shot). In 3D rotation math ([Launch Monitor Technology](../technology-launch-monitors.html#photometric-camera-systems)), matching the surface pattern across frames yields a rotation matrix $\Delta R \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ whose turn angle is $\theta = \arccos((\operatorname{tr}\Delta R - 1)/2)$, which divides by $\Delta t$ to give spin rate in rpm.
- **Reconstructing the clubhead (HMT and marker modes):** For the GC2, Foresight's [2023 Ball & Club Data Guide](https://support.foresightsports.com/sites/default/files/downloads/2023/2023%20Ball%20%26%20Club%20Data%20Doc.pdf) states that HMT Head Measurement Technology uses high-speed cameras to measure club speed, club path, angle of attack, face angle, loft, lie, closure rate, and impact location (**manufacturer claim**; in @Leach2017LaunchMonitor, GC2+HMT tracked reflective markers on the clubhead). On newer integrated Foresight units, the [club-marker guide](https://help.foresightsports.com/hc/en-us/articles/4408197030035-How-to-Apply-and-Maintain-Club-Markers-for-Foresight-Sports-Devices) distinguishes **one-marker** mode (GC3 and Launch Pro: club speed, club path, and angle of attack) from **four-marker** mode (GCQuad, QuadMAX, Falcon, and GCHawk: adding face angle, dynamic loft, lie angle, impact location, and closure rate; **manufacturer claim**; [Launch Monitor Vendor Reference](../launch-monitor-vendor-reference.html#foresight-sports-and-bushnell-launch-pro)).

### Doppler Radar and Hybrid Monitors (For Example, Rapsodo MLM2PRO and MLM2XPRO) {#sec-radar-architecture}

A **Doppler radar** monitor sits behind the golfer, looking down the target line. It uses the **Doppler effect**—the same physical principle that makes an ambulance siren sound higher-pitched as it approaches you and lower-pitched as it moves away, and the same way a police speed gun clocks a car.

- **Hardware and raw signals:** A **monostatic** radar (one where the transmitter and receiver share the same box) sends out radio waves of wavelength $\lambda = c/f_c$ and measures the frequency shift $f_d = 2\dot{d}/\lambda$ of the echoes bouncing back from the clubhead and ball ([Launch Monitor Technology](../technology-launch-monitors.html#doppler-radar)). Crucially, that frequency shift hears only **radial speed** ($\dot{d}$)—how fast the object is moving directly **toward or away from** the radar box. To tell whether the ball launched high or low, left or right, the radar compares the arrival timing (phase difference $\Delta\varphi$) of the returning wave across multiple receiver antennas inside the box, or pairs the radar with an optical camera.
- **Hybrid optical-radar fusion (manufacturer claims):** Many portable monitors combine Doppler radar with built-in cameras. According to the [Rapsodo Golf FAQ](https://rapsodo.com/pages/frequently-asked-golf-questions-faq) (**manufacturer claim**), the **Rapsodo MLM2PRO** and **MLM2XPRO** are placed $7.5\text{ feet}$ ($2$–$3\text{ paces}$) behind the ball on a level surface aligned with the target line, combining radar with dual optical cameras (Shot Vision and Impact Vision). In Rapsodo's **MLM2PRO** FAQ entry, the unit provides 15 metrics, of which **8 are labeled as `(measured)`** (**manufacturer claim**): ball speed, club speed, launch angle, launch direction, spin rate, spin axis, club path, and angle of attack. The **MLM2XPRO** FAQ entry states that the MLM2PRO and MLM2XPRO "provide the same metrics" (listing 14 metrics by name without repeating the `(measured)` labels or Shot Type; **manufacturer claim**).
- **Conditions on spin and face angle:** In the Rapsodo FAQ (**manufacturer claim**), spin rate and spin axis are measured only when using specially patterned Callaway or Titleist **RPT** (Rapsodo Precision Technology) balls (and, in the MLM2XPRO FAQ entry, with RPT selected in the **Net** environment and an active membership). Notably, **face angle is not among the metrics** reported by the MLM2PRO or MLM2XPRO (**manufacturer claim**). On pure radar systems that do report spin axis or face angle without marked balls, spin rate comes from periodic radar ripples as the ball turns, spin axis is either resolved from phase differences across the ball or worked out from how the ball curves in flight (using the aerodynamic lift acceleration $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{g} - \mathbf{D}$ after subtracting gravity $\mathbf{g}$ and air drag $\mathbf{D}$), and face angle is either constrained by radar reflections or worked out backward from ball start direction and club path ([Launch Monitor Technology](../technology-launch-monitors.html#spin-axis-from-flight)).

## Metric-by-Metric Breakdown: Measured Versus Inferred {#sec-metric-breakdown}

In general, **ball speed** and **launch angles** sit closest to what the sensors directly observe, whereas **face angle on a rear radar**, **spin axis without marked balls**, **smash factor**, and **carry distance** lean heaviest on models and assumptions. In @tbl-camera-vs-radar, the second column summarizes where each metric sits on that chain, and a dagger ($\dagger$) marks a **manufacturer claim** from the vendor's published documentation ([Foresight 2023 Ball & Club Data Guide](https://support.foresightsports.com/sites/default/files/downloads/2023/2023%20Ball%20%26%20Club%20Data%20Doc.pdf); [Rapsodo Golf FAQ](https://rapsodo.com/pages/frequently-asked-golf-questions-faq)).

| Metric | How Direct? | Camera Monitor (e.g., Foresight GC2 / GC2+HMT) | Radar / Hybrid Monitor (e.g., Rapsodo MLM2PRO / MLM2XPRO; Rear Radar) | Primary Error & Fragility Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ball Speed** | **Observed / geometric** | 3D ball displacement across calibrated high-speed stereo frames just after separation$^\dagger$. | Post-impact radial Doppler shift ($f_d = 2\dot{d}/\lambda$) combined with initial launch angle$^\dagger$. | Camera: stereo scale calibration, exposure blur, trigger timing. Radar: angle projection, short indoor travel before hitting a net. |
| **Launch Angle & Direction** | **Observed / geometric** | 3D direction of the initial ball-velocity vector relative to the unit's level and alignment$^\dagger$. | Radar receiver-array phase differences ($\Delta\varphi$) and optical camera tracking$^\dagger$. | If the unit is tilted or aimed $1^\circ$ off the target line, launch angle or direction shifts by $1^\circ$. |
| **Spin Rate & Spin Axis** | **Observed (camera / RPT) or Inferred (flight radar)** | Optical registration of ball surface pattern across flashes to measure 3D rotation$^\dagger$. | **MLM2PRO/2XPRO:** optically measured *only* with RPT-marked balls (in Net mode)$^\dagger$. **Pure radar:** spin rate from echo harmonics; spin axis often **inferred** from flight curve or phase structure. | Camera: dimple symmetry aliasing at high rpm, dirt or moisture. Radar (indoor net): too little flight time to see the ball curve. |
| **Club Speed** | **Observed (radar / HMT)** | **With HMT:** 3D speed of tracked clubface markers just before impact$^\dagger$. **Base GC2:** not observed. | Doppler frequency shift of radar echoes returning from the moving clubhead$^\dagger$. | Different reference points on the head (face center vs geometric center vs strongest radar reflection) move at different speeds. |
| **Club Path & Attack Angle** | **Observed (HMT / hybrid) + priors** | **With HMT:** 3D travel direction of tracked face markers$^\dagger$. | **MLM2PRO:** labeled as measured via radar + optical tracking$^\dagger$. **Single-station Doppler alone:** radial echoes provide at most 3 of 6 rigid-body motion components without extra views or geometric assumptions. | Reference-point velocity shift ($\mathbf{v}_P = \mathbf{v}_O + \boldsymbol{\omega}\times\mathbf{r}$): head center and face center can differ by a degree or more on a rotating driver; target-line alignment. |
| **Face Angle** | **Observed (HMT / 4-marker) or Model-inferred** | **With HMT (or 4-marker mode):** 3D plane fit to reflective markers on the clubface$^\dagger$. | **MLM2PRO/2XPRO:** not reported$^\dagger$. **Other rear radars:** often **inferred** by working backward from ball start direction and club path, or constrained via radar reflections. | Marker fit vs curved driver face; if worked out from ball launch, off-center strikes (gear effect) fool the formula. |
| **Smash Factor** | **Derived ratio** | **Calculated** as $s = v_{\mathrm{ball}} / v_{\mathrm{club}}$$^\dagger$. | **Calculated** as $s = v_{\mathrm{ball}} / v_{\mathrm{club}}$$^\dagger$. | Divides out between-golfer speed differences; combines errors from both speeds; sensitive to club-speed reference point. |
| **Carry Distance** | **Model-inferred (simulated)** | **Calculated** by running an aerodynamic flight model from initial launch and spin$^\dagger$. | **Calculated** from launch and spin$^\dagger$. Even outdoor full-flight radar depends on landing definitions and extrapolation when bounce is not directly observed. | Sensitive to spin-rate and spin-axis errors, aerodynamic drag/lift models, and unmeasured wind, temperature, or altitude. |

### Single-Shot Accuracy Against a Reference Standard {#sec-independent-benchmarks}

A vendor label of "measured" does not mean every parameter has the same accuracy. To test **single-shot accuracy** (how closely a monitor agrees with an independent truth standard on the same shot), @Leach2017LaunchMonitor compared a stereoscopic camera system (Foresight GC2+HMT) and a Doppler radar system (TrackMan Pro IIIe) simultaneously against a calibrated high-speed GOM optical reference across 240 attempted shots (8 golfers, driver, 7-iron, and utility wedge; data collected in January 2015).

Both systems agreed generally more closely with the reference on **ball parameters** (ball speed, launch angle, launch direction, and spin rate) than on **clubhead parameters** (club speed, club direction, attack angle, and face angle). In Table 6 of @Leach2017LaunchMonitor, the authors reported the percentage of retained shots falling within a **median-centered band**—meaning within $\pm 1\text{ mph}$ or $\pm 1^\circ$ of *each device's own typical offset* (median difference) from the reference. A median-centered band measures **consistency around the device's bias, not closeness to zero error**: as noted in [Launch Monitor Vendor Reference](../launch-monitor-vendor-reference.html#a-small-statistical-counterexample), if a device read every shot between $4.9^\circ$ and $5.1^\circ$ too high, $100\%$ of its shots would fall within $\pm 1^\circ$ of its median ($+5.0^\circ$), even though none was within $1^\circ$ of the true angle. Within those median-centered research bands, TrackMan fell inside $\pm 1\text{ mph}$ on 54% of shots for clubhead speed versus 29% for Foresight; within $\pm 1^\circ$ for club direction, TrackMan achieved 45% and Foresight 58%; within $\pm 1^\circ$ for face angle, TrackMan achieved 66% and Foresight 26% (with median face-angle differences of $0.0^\circ$ and $-0.8^\circ$, respectively). TrackMan returned club data on 62% of attempted shots (only 19% with the wedge), whereas Foresight returned club data on 75% ([Launch Monitor Vendor Reference](../launch-monitor-vendor-reference.html#iv.1-the-traceable-benchmark-study-located)). These are historical, protocol-specific results from 2015 hardware and firmware, not current product rankings.

For the Rapsodo MLM2PRO, Rapsodo published a [June 2025 club-data comparison with a Foresight GCQuad](https://rapsodo.com/blogs/golf/mlm2pro-vs-foresight-gcquad-clubdata) across 1,021 shots (**manufacturer claim**), reporting mean absolute differences of $1.05^\circ$ for attack angle and $1.19^\circ$ for club path ([Launch Monitor Vendor Reference](../launch-monitor-vendor-reference.html#rapsodo-mlm2pro)). As with any two-device comparison, a mean absolute difference is an average gap rather than a maximum error or 95% interval, and the comparator's own uncertainty, shared alignment, and excluded shots must be kept in mind.

## Week-to-Week Repeatability: The Bright et al. (2026) Study {#sec-bright-study}

Single-shot accuracy against a laboratory camera is only half of the story. Golfers, coaches, and researchers also use launch monitors to track whether a player's swing or physical training is improving from one week to the next. Why bring a jumping study into an article about launch monitors? A recent paper by @Bright2026CMJDriving in *Sports* ([doi:10.3390/sports14100439](https://doi.org/10.3390/sports14100439)) examined whether lower-body jumping power is associated with driving performance—and to check their measurements, the authors tested 28 skilled golfers on a launch monitor across two sessions one week apart. We borrow their **between-session reliability** results, which show a striking contrast between clubhead speed, ball speed, and smash factor.

### Study Design and Method {#sec-bright-method}

@Bright2026CMJDriving examined whether countermovement jump (CMJ—a standing vertical jump where the athlete dips down and immediately jumps as high and fast as possible) force–time variables were associated with driver clubhead speed, ball speed, and smash factor across the performance distribution (25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles), and whether those associations stayed consistent across two sessions:

- **Participants:** $n = 28$ sub-elite male golfers (age $19.9 \pm 1.0\text{ years}$, stature $1.80 \pm 0.06\text{ m}$, body mass $76.6 \pm 13.9\text{ kg}$, handicap $0.8 \pm 1.9$).
- **Protocol:** Two identical testing sessions separated by one week at the same time of day in a private indoor swing studio. In each session, golfers completed three maximal CMJs on a force platform (Bertec 5060-06 at $1000\text{ Hz}$, processed in Hawkin Dynamics software) to measure jump height, jump momentum (body mass times take-off velocity), and peak propulsive power.
- **Launch monitor setup:** Golfers hit maximal-effort drives with their own custom-fitted drivers and Titleist Pro V1 balls off artificial grass into an indoor net. A **TrackMan 4** (operated in Indoor Mode) was placed $2.7\text{ m}$ ($\approx 8.9\text{ feet}$) behind the golfer, level with the hitting mat and aligned with the target. Three valid shots per golfer per session were retained ($168$ total drives). Importantly, centeredness of strike was judged from sound, feel, and ball-flight feedback by the golfer and investigator, rather than measured objectively with impact tape or face-location cameras.
- **How repeatability was scored (CV vs ICC):** Before looking at the numbers, it helps to separate the two repeatability scores used in sports science.[^bright-bayes]
  - **CV% (coefficient of variation — absolute reliability)** asks: *how much does an individual golfer's number wobble from shot to shot and session to session, as a percentage of the group average?* A small CV% means each golfer's readings stay close to their own typical value.
  - **ICC (intraclass correlation coefficient — relative reliability)** asks: *if we rank the 28 golfers from highest to lowest in Session 1, do they come out in the same order in Session 2?* ICC runs from $0$ (the ranking is completely scrambled next week) to $1$ (the ranking is identical). Imagine measuring the heights of a basketball squad where everyone stands between $1.99\text{ m}$ and $2.01\text{ m}$: even if your tape measure is accurate to within $0.5\%$ (excellent CV%), a tiny change in posture or tape placement will completely shuffle who measures tallest from one week to the next (poor ICC).
  - **Crucial caveat:** In repeated human swings, both CV% and ICC mix **the golfer's own biological shot-to-shot and day-to-day variation** (including strike location on the clubface) with **the launch monitor's measurement error**. @Bright2026CMJDriving cannot separate golfer variation from sensor noise, and the study used one radar unit only.

[^bright-bayes]: @Bright2026CMJDriving fitted Bayesian variance-components models (`brms` in R: $\text{variable} \sim 1 + \text{session} + (1 \mid \text{participant})$) to the 168 trial-level observations using weakly informative priors, computing $\mathrm{ICC} = \sigma_{\mathrm{between}}^2 / (\sigma_{\mathrm{between}}^2 + \sigma_{\mathrm{within}}^2)$ and $\mathrm{CV}\% = (\sigma_{\mathrm{residual}} / \text{grand mean}) \times 100$ across posterior draws. They rated ICC by the lower bound of its 95% credible interval (CrI) as poor ($<0.50$), moderate ($0.50$–$0.74$), good ($0.75$–$0.90$), or excellent ($>0.90$), and CV% by its upper 95% CrI bound as excellent ($<5\%$). Predictor–outcome slopes across the 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles were estimated with Bayesian quantile regression (asymmetric Laplace likelihood).

### Empirical Results: High Club-Speed Reliability, Poor Smash Factor Rank-Order Reliability {#sec-bright-results}

@tbl-bright-reliability reproduces the between-session reliability and descriptive statistics from Tables 1 and 2 of @Bright2026CMJDriving.

| Variable | Session 1 Mean $\pm$ SD | Session 2 Mean $\pm$ SD | Rank-Order Repeatability: ICC [95% CrI] | Within-Golfer Wobble: CV% [95% CrI] | Study Rating (by 95% CrI Bound) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Clubhead Speed** (mph) | $112.33 \pm 6.15$ | $112.34 \pm 6.35$ | $0.98\;[0.96, 0.99]$ | $0.90\;[0.80, 1.02]$ | Excellent ICC, Excellent CV |
| **Ball Speed** (mph) | $162.40 \pm 9.01$ | $162.22 \pm 8.87$ | $0.81\;[0.71, 0.90]$ | $2.42\;[2.15, 2.73]$ | Moderate ICC, Excellent CV |
| **Smash Factor** ($v_b / v_c$) | $1.45 \pm 0.04$ | $1.44 \pm 0.04$ | $0.24\;[0.00, 0.57]$ | $1.72\;[1.33, 2.21]$ | **Poor ICC**, Excellent CV |
| **Jump Height** (m) | $0.29 \pm 0.07$ | $0.29 \pm 0.06$ | $0.98\;[0.96, 0.99]$ | $3.40\;[3.03, 3.83]$ | Excellent ICC, Excellent CV |
| **Jump Momentum** ($\mathrm{kg\cdot m/s}$) | $181.16 \pm 31.94$ | $180.69 \pm 29.92$ | $0.98\;[0.96, 0.99]$ | $1.84\;[1.64, 2.07]$ | Excellent ICC, Excellent CV |
| **Peak Propulsive Power** (W) | $3414.70 \pm 590.03$ | $3406.71 \pm 550.74$ | $0.99\;[0.99, 1.00]$ | $2.80\;[2.48, 3.19]$ | Excellent ICC, Excellent CV |

: Between-session reliability and descriptive statistics across two sessions one week apart in $n = 28$ sub-elite male golfers ($168$ trials), reproduced from Tables 1 and 2 of @Bright2026CMJDriving. {#tbl-bright-reliability}

Three practical findings stand out:

1. **Clubhead speed was highly repeatable both within and between golfers:** Relative reliability was excellent ($\mathrm{ICC} = 0.98\;[0.96, 0.99]$) and within-golfer percentage wobble was under one percent ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.90\%$). Across the group, clubhead speed spanned a wide range (quantile means from $104$–$105\text{ mph}$ in the bottom quarter to $122\text{ mph}$ in the top 10%, with descriptive $\mathrm{SD} \approx 6.2\text{ mph}$). Jump momentum and peak propulsive power showed consistent positive associations with clubhead speed in both sessions. The jump-height slope weakened in Session 2 at the 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles ($98$–$99\%$ posterior probability of a decrease), which the authors note *may partly reflect* that jump height is independent of body mass, whereas jump momentum and peak propulsive power scale with body mass (a trait that stays stable across a one-week gap).
2. **Ball speed dropped to moderate rank-order repeatability:** While still below $3\%$ in percentage wobble ($\mathrm{CV} = 2.42\%$), ball speed had the largest CV% of the three golf variables and a moderate relative reliability ($\mathrm{ICC} = 0.81\;[0.71, 0.90]$). Associations between the jump variables and ball speed were uncertain across all quantiles and both sessions, with 95% credible intervals spanning zero in every quantile model.
3. **Smash factor had poor rank-order repeatability ($\mathrm{ICC} = 0.24\;[0.00, 0.57]$):** Even though each golfer's smash factor stayed within a tight percentage band ($\mathrm{CV} = 1.72\%\;[1.33, 2.21]$), a golfer's smash-factor ranking in Session 1 told little about their ranking in Session 2 (the 95% credible interval for ICC reached $0.00$). Quantile regression slopes against smash factor were uniformly trivial ($-0.005$ to $0.005$) and Bayesian correlations spanned zero ($r = -0.30$ to $0.08$).

Why did smash factor's ICC drop to $0.24$ when its two ingredients had ICCs of $0.98$ and $0.81$? @Bright2026CMJDriving note that the weaker associations for ball speed and smash factor *may be partly explained* by their lower between-session relative reliability, and that for smash factor specifically, poor relative reliability *likely also reflects* the technical homogeneity of this sub-elite sample—whose scores were closely clustered between $1.40$ and $1.50$ (descriptive $\mathrm{SD} = 0.04$), restricting the between-individual range [@Hopkins2009ProgressiveStatistics]—which is *further complicated* by smash factor being a derived ratio ($v_b / v_c$), so measurement error in either component propagates into the ratio [@Atkinson1998Reliability].

## Error Propagation and Range Restriction in Derived Metrics {#sec-error-propagation}

### How Errors Enter Smash Factor and Why Bunching Drives the Low ICC {#sec-smash-jacobian}

In plain terms, smash factor ($s = v_b / v_c$) reads high if ball speed ($v_b$) is a bit higher than usual *or* if clubhead speed ($v_c$) is read a bit lower than usual—just as a car's miles-per-gallon figure jumps when the odometer reads high and the fuel used is under-counted on the same trip. If both errors happen in opposite directions on the same shot, they add together.

For engineers, a first-order Taylor (tangent or **Jacobian**) expansion around a typical shot $(\bar{v}_b, \bar{v}_c)$ with nominal smash factor $\bar{s} = \bar{v}_b / \bar{v}_c$ writes a small change $\delta s$ in smash factor in terms of small changes $\delta v_b$ and $\delta v_c$:

$$
\delta s \approx J_s \begin{bmatrix} \delta v_b \\ \delta v_c \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial s}{\partial v_b} & \dfrac{\partial s}{\partial v_c} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \delta v_b \\ \delta v_c \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\bar{v}_c}\,\delta v_b - \frac{\bar{v}_b}{\bar{v}_c^2}\,\delta v_c = \bar{s}\left(\frac{\delta v_b}{\bar{v}_b} - \frac{\delta v_c}{\bar{v}_c}\right).
$$ {#eq-smash-jacobian}

Evaluating @eq-smash-jacobian at the Session 1 average of @Bright2026CMJDriving ($\bar{v}_c = 112.33\text{ mph}$, $\bar{v}_b = 162.40\text{ mph}$, $\bar{s} \approx 1.4457$) gives the per-mph sensitivities:

$$
\frac{\partial s}{\partial v_b} = \frac{1}{112.33} \approx +0.00890\text{ mph}^{-1}, \qquad \frac{\partial s}{\partial v_c} = -\frac{162.40}{112.33^2} \approx -0.01287\text{ mph}^{-1}.
$$ {#eq-smash-gradients}

Notice two things in @eq-smash-jacobian and @eq-smash-gradients:

1. **Per percent, the two speeds carry equal weight; per mph, clubhead speed is $1.45\times$ steeper:** Because $\bar{v}_b$ is $1.45\times$ larger than $\bar{v}_c$, a $1\%$ error in either speed moves smash factor by the same amount ($\approx 0.0145$), whereas a $1\text{ mph}$ error in clubhead speed moves smash factor $1.45\times$ as much as a $1\text{ mph}$ error in ball speed. If a shot happens to have a $+1.0\text{ mph}$ error in ball speed and a $-1.0\text{ mph}$ error in clubhead speed at the same time, reported smash factor jumps by $\delta s \approx +0.022$ (say, from $1.450$ to $1.472$)—more than half of the entire descriptive standard deviation ($0.04$) in the sub-elite sample. As noted in [Metric-by-Metric Breakdown](#sec-metric-breakdown), any shot-to-shot shift in which point on the clubhead the radar tracks will enter $\delta v_c$ with this $-0.0129\text{ mph}^{-1}$ slope.
2. **Across shots, correlated speeds make smash factor's percentage wobble *smaller*, not larger:** From the right-hand side of @eq-smash-jacobian, the percentage variance ($\mathrm{CV}^2$) of smash factor relates to the percentage variances of ball speed and clubhead speed and their within-golfer correlation $\rho_{bc}$ by:

$$
\mathrm{CV}_s^2 \approx \mathrm{CV}_{v_b}^2 + \mathrm{CV}_{v_c}^2 - 2\rho_{bc}\,\mathrm{CV}_{v_b}\,\mathrm{CV}_{v_c}.
$$ {#eq-smash-cv}

If ball speed and clubhead speed varied independently ($\rho_{bc} = 0$), smash factor's CV would be $\sqrt{2.42^2 + 0.90^2} \approx 2.58\%$, larger than either input. Instead, in @Bright2026CMJDriving, $\mathrm{CV}_s = 1.72\%$, which is *smaller* than ball speed's $\mathrm{CV}_{v_b} = 2.42\%$. Plugging those three published CVs into @eq-smash-cv implies a strong positive within-golfer correlation ($\rho_{bc} \approx 0.85$, implied by @eq-smash-cv rather than reported directly by @Bright2026CMJDriving)—when a player swings a little faster, the ball leaves a little faster too, and the ratio cancels that shared swing-speed fluctuation.

So why is the rank-order repeatability ($\mathrm{ICC} = 0.24$) so poor? Look at the variance-components ratio that defines ICC:

$$
\mathrm{ICC}(s) = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{between}}^2(s)}{\sigma_{\mathrm{between}}^2(s) + \sigma_{\mathrm{within}}^2(s)}.
$$ {#eq-icc-collapse}

Dividing $v_b$ by $v_c$ cancels out the large, stable speed differences across golfers (clubhead speed had a descriptive $\mathrm{SD} \approx 6.2\text{ mph}$, supporting an $\mathrm{ICC}$ of $0.98$). In this technically homogeneous sub-elite cohort, smash factors were tightly bunched (descriptive $\mathrm{SD} = 0.04$, quantile averages $1.40$ to $1.50$), which @Bright2026CMJDriving suggest likely contributes to the low ICC. Meanwhile, the within-golfer residual $\sigma_{\mathrm{within}}(s) \approx 0.025$ ($1.72\%$ of $1.45$) retains every unshared fluctuation between the two speeds:

- **Strike-location and face-to-path variation** ($\delta v_b$ at fixed $v_c$): a few millimeters of heel/toe or high/low strike shift ball speed via off-center gear effect and energy loss [@Betzler2014DriverPresentation] without changing pre-impact clubhead speed.
- **Uncorrelated sensor noise** ($\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_b, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_c$): independent measurement errors in the two speeds do not cancel; their variances add ($\sigma_{\epsilon,s}^2 = \bar{v}_c^{-2}\sigma_{\epsilon,b}^2 + \bar{s}^2\bar{v}_c^{-2}\sigma_{\epsilon,c}^2$).

This tight bunching is consistent with a low ICC.[^icc-note] A low $\mathrm{CV}\%$ ($1.72\%$) only says that everyone's smash factor stays close to $1.45$; it does **not** mean smash factor can reliably rank skilled golfers from one week to the next.

[^icc-note]: As a quick check on the published summary numbers, plugging the residual standard deviation $\sigma_{\mathrm{within}} \approx 0.0172 \times 1.45 \approx 0.025$ and the descriptive total $\mathrm{SD}$ from Table 2 into $1 - \sigma_{\mathrm{within}}^2 / \mathrm{SD}^2$ reproduces the reported ICC closely for clubhead speed ($\approx 0.97$ vs $0.98$) and ball speed ($\approx 0.81$ vs $0.81$), whereas using the rounded descriptive $\mathrm{SD} = 0.04$ for smash factor gives $\approx 0.61$ (or $\approx 0.49$ if $\mathrm{SD} = 0.035$ before rounding). The $\mathrm{ICC} = 0.24\;[0.00, 0.57]$ reported here is the posterior median from @Bright2026CMJDriving's trial-level Bayesian variance-components model (`brms`), not a hand calculation from the rounded descriptive table.

### How Working Backward From Ball Launch Amplifies Face-Angle Errors {#sec-angle-jacobian}

While smash factor's percentage spread is damped by correlated speeds, **working backward through a model** genuinely magnifies errors. Consider how golf's familiar launch-direction rule works. With a **centered driver strike** in the horizontal plane, empirical testing by @Wood2018FacePathLaunch and @Henrikson2020TangentialCompliance found that the ball's initial horizontal start direction ($\ell$) starts roughly three-quarters of the way ($w \approx 0.76 \pm 0.08$, 95% confidence interval) toward where the clubface points ($f$) and one-quarter toward the club path ($p$): $\ell \approx w f + (1-w)p$.

If a rear-mounted launch monitor does not directly observe the clubface plane and instead works backward from measured ball start direction $\ell$ and measured club path $p$ to *infer* face angle $f$, it must solve that equation in reverse ([Launch Monitor Technology](../technology-launch-monitors.html#face-inference-from-a-declared-launch-model)):

$$
f(\ell, p, w) = p + \frac{\ell - p}{w}, \qquad \nabla f = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \ell} & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial p} & \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial w} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{w} & 1 - \dfrac{1}{w} & -\dfrac{\ell - p}{w^2} \end{bmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-face-inversion}

Here $\nabla f$ is the sensitivity vector (gradient) showing how errors in $(\ell, p, w)$ feed into the inferred face angle:

- **Launch-error amplification ($1/w \approx 1.316$):** Because $w \approx 0.76$ is in the denominator, any measurement error in ball start direction $\ell$ is multiplied by $1/0.76 \approx 1.32$ (about $32\%$ amplification).
- **Off-center strike misattribution:** The weight $w \approx 0.76$ was fitted on centered driver strikes. If you hit the ball toward the toe or heel, **gear effect** (the twisting of the clubhead around its center of gravity during off-center impact) changes the ball's start direction $\ell$ and spin. A monitor that blindly plugs that shifted start direction $\ell$ into @eq-face-inversion has no way to know the strike was off-center, so it blames the start direction on an open or closed clubface $f$.
- **Camera marker trade-offs:** A stereoscopic camera system with multiple face markers (such as GC2+HMT) avoids inverting @eq-face-inversion, but substitutes a geometric sensitivity of its own: how well a flat plane fitted to the reflective stickers matches the **contact normal** (the direction the face points at the exact spot of impact) across a driver face curved with **bulge and roll** (the slight toe-to-heel and crown-to-sole curvature of a wood face; see [Launch Monitor Vendor Reference](../launch-monitor-vendor-reference.html#iii.3-nobody-actually-measures-the-centre-of-gravity)).

## Connection to AffineDrift: Sensitivity and Inferred Versus Observed State {#sec-affinedrift-connection}

*This section connects launch monitor equations to the mathematical framework used across the rest of AffineDrift; golfers looking for practical takeaways can skip directly to @sec-practical-checklist.*

Launch monitor literacy is the measurement-side mirror of AffineDrift's core mechanical theme:

1. **Inferred state is only as good as the observation map and the prior model:** Just as net joint torques from [inverse dynamics](../inverse-dynamics.html) cannot uniquely identify individual muscle forces or two-hand grip forces that lie in the **null space** of the grasp map—combinations of hidden forces that cancel out and produce zero change in what the outside sensor sees ([After One Solution](../after-one-solution-null-space-exploration.html))—a launch monitor's raw observables ($\mathbf{z}$) leave blind spots unless extra camera views, club/ball markers (HMT stickers, RPT patterns), or model assumptions close the equations. When a vendor closes that gap with a model assumption, the displayed number moves from an *observed state* to an *inferred state*.
2. **Tangent-space sensitivity governs what survives noise:** In our downswing dynamics series ([Part 2: Dynamics](../tangent-hyperplanes-series/part-2-dynamics.html)), small state perturbations propagate through the state-transition map $\Phi$ and task Jacobian $J$ as $\Sigma_y = J \Sigma_x J^{\mathsf T}$. At the launch monitor boundary, the same first-order covariance law (@eq-smash-cv and @eq-face-inversion) governs derived outputs. @Bright2026CMJDriving note that smash factor "may also be unsuitable as a primary monitoring outcome in repeated-measures designs." More broadly in AffineDrift's framework, treating a derived ratio or a model-inferred angle as if it were a direct, noise-free state measurement can obscure real physical relationships or mistake small strike and measurement fluctuations for swing changes.

## Practical Checklist for Golfers and Engineers {#sec-practical-checklist}

- **Separate single-shot accuracy from week-to-week golfer repeatability:**
  - *Single-shot accuracy against a reference camera* (@Leach2017LaunchMonitor): On both camera and radar monitors, ball launch numbers (ball speed, launch angle, launch direction, and spin rate) agreed generally more closely with the reference standard than clubhead numbers did.
  - *Week-to-week repeatability in skilled golfers* (@Bright2026CMJDriving): **Clubhead speed** was the most repeatable swing metric ($\mathrm{ICC} = 0.98$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.90\%$), **ball speed** had moderate rank-order repeatability ($\mathrm{ICC} = 0.81$, $\mathrm{CV} = 2.42\%$), likely partly because it also reflects shot-to-shot strike quality and face control, and **smash factor** had poor rank-order repeatability ($\mathrm{ICC} = 0.24$). Follow @Bright2026CMJDriving in prioritizing clubhead speed when tracking physical development across sessions (where smash factor "may also be unsuitable as a primary monitoring outcome"), and always pair ball speed with strike-location feedback (such as face spray or optical impact location).
- **Check your unit's marker, ball, and environment rules:** Before trusting spin or club numbers, check whether your device requires patterned balls (such as RPT balls in Net mode on the Rapsodo MLM2PRO/MLM2XPRO; **manufacturer claim**) or clubhead attachments and multi-marker setups (such as HMT on the Foresight GC2; **manufacturer claim**).
- **Match reference points before comparing club path across devices:** A geometric-center club path on a radar unit and a face-center path on a camera unit can differ by a degree or more on the exact same physical swing depending on clubhead rotation (about $1.3^\circ$ in the worked example of [The Reference-Point Problem](../reference-point-problem.html#a-reproducible-perpendicular-example), and roughly $3^\circ$ in TrackMan's [illustrative driver example](https://www.trackman.com/blog/club-data-definitions)).
